title: The world's kitchen on a street corner
text: Street food has travelled {{1}} migrants for as long as there have been cities, and {{2}} was once hawkers' grub is now a term of praise. {{3}} recent years, covered markets devoted to it have opened in cities from London to Singapore, halls {{4}} a dozen cuisines share one roof and one long, happy queue. The food is half the attraction; the other half is the theatre of watching {{5}} be made in front of you by cooks who have, quite possibly, invented the dish in {{6}} own kitchen. The same dishes cost twice {{7}} much across the street in a restaurant, {{8}} nobody seems to mind paying for the ceiling. What the market ultimately sells is company: eating standing up, elbow to elbow with strangers, is the oldest dinner party there is.

gaps.explanation: Fused relative subject: what was once.
'In recent years' is the fixed phrase.

gaps.hint: relative adverb: halls ___ a dozen cuisines share
gaps.explanation: 'Where' refers back to the halls as the place.

gaps.hint: pronoun: watching ___ be made in front
gaps.explanation: Object pronoun referring to the food: watching it.
The kitchen belongs to the cooks: their own.
'Twice as much' — the fixed comparative frame.

gaps.hint: conjunction: costs twice as much, ___ nobody minds
gaps.explanation: Contrast between price and indifference: but.
